definition: The ugly duckling theorem is an argument showing that classification is not really possible without some sort of bias.
details: More particularly, it assumes finitely many properties combinable by logical connectives, and finitely many objects; it asserts that any two different objects share the same number of (extensional) properties. The theorem is named after Hans Christian Andersen's 1843 story "The Ugly Duckling", because it shows that a duckling is just as similar to a swan as two swans are to each other. It was derived by Satosi Watanabe in 1969.
story: Picture a parachute packed by a second pair of hands: nobody plans to need it, but everyone is glad it was checked. Think of it this way: The ugly duckling theorem is an argument showing that classification is not really possible without some sort of bias. And here is the clever part: More particularly, it assumes finitely many properties combinable by logical connectives, and finitely many objects; it asserts that any two different objects share the same number of (extensional) properties. Caution is not the enemy of progress — it is the reason progress gets to keep going. And that is Ugly duckling theorem — the reason we can move fast without breaking things, or people.
